title: Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11)
hook: the king sees, takes, and arranges a loyal husband's death

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonathan's son received David's chesed, sitting at his table, lame in both feet, a place kept for him always. Your line was always at my table. Did you make a place for someone? Today, the same king, in a chapter that turns against him. Day seven hundred forty-six.

At the turn of the year, the text says, the time when kings go out to battle. So David sends his general Joab, and his servants, and the whole army. And David stays in Jerusalem. That one detail sits at the start of the chapter like a stone in a shoe. The king isn't where kings go. One evening he gets up from his bed and walks on the roof of the king's house. And from the roof he sees a woman washing herself, and she is very beautiful. He doesn't look away. He sends someone to find out who she is.
screen: `WHEN KINGS GO OUT TO BATTLE.` → `DAVID STAYS IN JERUSALEM.` → `A WOMAN SEEN FROM THE ROOF.`

segments.voice: The answer comes back with names: Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam, wife of Uriah the Hittite. Married. Her husband is away, fighting in David's own army. Listen to the verbs that follow, all of them the king's. He sees. He sends. He takes. The text gives Bathsheba almost no words in this chapter. The few she sends are a message: I am with child. Then David starts covering. He calls Uriah home from the front and tells him, go down to your house. Uriah doesn't. He sleeps at the palace door with the servants. When David asks why, Uriah says the ark and Israel and Judah are living in tents, and my lord Joab is camped in the open field. How could I go home, eat and drink, and lie with my wife? David gets him drunk. He still won't go home. So David writes a letter to Joab and sends it with Uriah himself. Put Uriah in the front of the hardest fighting, then pull back from him, so he's struck down. Uriah carries his own death in his hand. It happens. Word comes back. And David sends a reply to Joab that sounds almost calm: don't let this thing be evil in your eyes. The sword devours one as well as another. Bathsheba mourns her husband. Then David brings her into his house. And the narrator, who has said nothing about right and wrong all chapter, speaks once: "But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD." In Hebrew it's an echo. David said, let it not be evil in your eyes. The narrator says, it was evil in the eyes of the Lord. The king could see a woman on a roof. He couldn't see what he was doing.
screen: `HE SEES. HE SENDS. HE TAKES.` · `URIAH WON'T GO HOME.` · `THE LETTER IN URIAH'S HAND.` · then, large: `IT DISPLEASED THE LORD.` · then: `HE COULDN'T SEE HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one way power blinds. Power turns up in ordinary places. Over a child, a younger sibling, an employee, a waiter, a partner who needs you, someone who owes you. Settle, and breathe. Let one of those places come to mind. Then ask, quietly: where might my power stop me from seeing this person clearly? What do I get to not notice, because I don't have to? Don't punish yourself. Just find one thing, and name it to yourself in a few words. If you pray, you can hold it before God. The bell holds the time.
Bathsheba. The woman the king saw, sent for and took, while her loyal husband slept at the palace door. Today's word.
Your line: power can blind. Today, look once more at the person you named, and do one thing that treats them as fully seen. Day seven hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Jews read the story of David and Bathsheba in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, and the next chapter, the prophet Nathan's rebuke, is read as part of the same story.

original.note: Hebrew: Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam and wife of Uriah, in 2 Samuel 11:3.

trapdoor: what you thought: a love story with a sad turn.
what it means: a king who stayed home sees, sends and takes, then arranges a loyal husband's death to hide it.
what a scholar hears: David says let this thing not be evil in your eyes; the narrator answers, it was evil in the eyes of the Lord.
recall: the glory is departed from Israel

sources.quoted: But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.

notes: Verify JPS 1917 wording of 2 Samuel 11:27 (certain in the KJV).
The Hebrew echo between 11:25 (al yera b'eineikha) and 11:27 (vayera ... b'einei) is stated; please confirm.
'At the turn of the year' paraphrases 11:1 ('the return of the year').
Bathsheba is presented without blame; the text gives her few words (11:5). Rabbinic readings that soften David's guilt (e.g. Shabbat 56a) are left out; a Keeper may want to add one.
Nathan's parable is left for the next day.
Editor: cut the invented 'he can see a lot of the city' (11:2 says only 'from the roof'), and softened the sweeping 'everyone has power somewhere' in the practice.
